chapter_theme: The poet turns to the rival king Acuvakanthan, whose temper and pleasures are named; his astrologer Satavintu warns him of pride and neglect and of the younger Podanam prince, and the king, boasting of his own strength, waves the warning away and tells his counsellors to speak.

cast.role: the rival king of the discus, taken as the one the astrologer addresses
Acuvakanthan's astrologer (நிமித்திகன்), who counsels and warns him
the learned counsellors of the rival king

620.reading: The poet says that a king who destroys in anger without weighing a matter and cannot bear an opposing word, and who, whenever his mind clears, thinks he can see through everyone, is carried along by his pride.
620.nuance: The poet opens the rival's portrait with his temper, ahead of the scene that shows it; the closing phrase of the verse is read as the poet's own name for such a king.

claims.claim: a king who strikes in anger without examining the matter is carried off by his own pride

621.reading: While the king plays with the garlanded women in the pond, the goddess of fortune, left unembraced, takes offence and looks for a place to go.
621.nuance: The verse says only that she looks for a place, not that she has gone; it is read as a forecast of loss, and sets the pond scene against the sleeplessness the envoy praised in 599.
621.event: The king's pleasure in the pond costs him the favour of the goddess of fortune, who begins to look elsewhere.

claims.claim: a king's wealth leaves him when he neglects it for pleasure

622.reading: One day the king's astrologer Satavintu, a sea of learning with unfading fame, speaks to the king of the strong anklets.
622.nuance: This is the second court in the poem to hear an astrologer; in 103 to 109 the Podanam king's astrologer reads a dream, and here the rival's astrologer reads the same fortune from the other side.
622.event: Satavintu, the astrologer of the rival king, begins to speak to him.

623.reading: The astrologer addresses the king and says that among those who rule the sea-ringed land there are said to be six hostile groups, which must be conquered first.
623.nuance: The verse does not say whether the six are outer rivals or inner faults; the next verse, which speaks of one who has conquered himself, is the only hint that the poet means the latter.

claims.claim: a ruler must first overcome six classes of foe

624.reading: The astrologer says that a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer, and that gold rains in the land where he rules.

claims.claim: a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer
the land of a self-mastering king is rich, as if gold rained on it

625.reading: The astrologer says that if the king stays with a sceptre without fault he will rule gladly, and the other kings, praising him, will serve under him.
625.nuance: The words for the sceptre and the rod are doubled and the grammar is clipped, so the sense of the condition is a best reading.

claims.claim: a king ruling with a faultless sceptre rules in ease and wins the praise of other kings

626.reading: The astrologer says the learned man who keeps what he has earned, draws in what he has not yet, guards the great wealth and gives it away becomes the guardian of others.

claims.claim: a learned king who earns, guards and gives wealth becomes the protector of others

627.reading: The astrologer says that pride is the dense frost which, if it falls, destroys the lotus of wealth that blooms in the water of one's own understanding.
627.nuance: The sun in the first line is the king's own knowledge, so the image makes understanding both the cause of wealth and the thing pride darkens.

claims.claim: pride destroys the wealth that understanding has built

628.reading: The astrologer says the king should think of those ruined by negligence, and be watchful in the hour of his own strength, as the books of praise say.
628.nuance: The counsel keeps close to Kural 539 in sense and in the pairing of joy and ruin, but the words are not those of the couplet, so no echo is marked; the verse names its source as the books of praise.

claims.claim: those ruined by negligence should be remembered when one is strong and glad

629.reading: The astrologer says the king already knows the even-handed justice of the right way, but that, though the king may be angered, he will speak what is for the king's good.

claims.claim: a counsellor must say what is for the king's good even at the risk of his anger

630.reading: On hearing him the king, wreathed in flowers, says he should speak well and bends his ear, the earring on his strong shoulder shedding light.
630.event: The king tells the astrologer to speak and bends his ear to listen.

631.reading: The astrologer tells the king to look at the sons of the king who rules the great city of Podanam, men like the god of love.
631.nuance: The verse names the princes' beauty and not yet the danger; the warning is in 632.
631.event: Satavintu points the king to the princes of Podanam as the matter of his warning.

632.reading: The astrologer says the youngest of those strong-shouldered princes will become our ancient enemy, and asks whether a petty word of omen should make him weaken at heart.
632.nuance: Who speaks the second half, and whether the closing question is the astrologer's own or his report of the king's coming mood, is not clear from the Tamil.
632.event: Satavintu names the younger Podanam prince as the foe the omen points to.

633.reading: The crowned king, told to weigh a fit course, waves the matter away with the shining palm of his hand.
633.nuance: The first two lines are hard to parse; the gesture of the palm is clear, and the rest is read as the astrologer's urging.
633.event: The king waves off the astrologer's advice with his hand.

634.reading: The king smiles and says that his shoulders have conquered the whole host of Vidyadhara kings, so what can other foes do against him.
634.nuance: The boast is the very pride that 627 warned of, spoken by the one warned, and 635 to 640 continue it.

claims.claim: a king who has beaten many kings need not fear lesser foes

635.reading: The king asks whether Mount Meru would shake at the fanning of a palm leaf, and so whether the strength of mere humans can disturb his faultless shoulders.
635.nuance: The boast holds that his own strength is what stands in the way, and that mortal men are the leaf beside the mountain.

636.reading: The king asks whether a great elephant's tusk blunts on a plantain stem, and so whether his shoulders, which slew the armies of the Danavas, would bend to men.

637.reading: The king asks whether a handful of small clouds can march against a fast wind, and so whether men, as his foes, could stir against his fury.

638.reading: The king says that if Indra's thunderbolt were set against him it would still fall short, and that if he turned his mind to his fierce shining discus he could cut down the shoulders of the gods.
638.nuance: The discus is the weapon 402 says Tivittan will take from him with his life; the boast is placed so that the reader hears that prophecy beneath it.

639.reading: The king asks whether, if he wished to send a spell against them, anyone could stand fearless, unless the book of omens is a deceit, and he calls the speaker one of angry nature.
639.nuance: The grammar of the question can be read as a challenge to the astrologer or as the king's wavering over the omen; the second reading is the more cautious.

claims.claim: the book of omens may be false

640.reading: The king says he has not been one to obey the word of the learned, and that he would fear only a petty word; even if the whole world rose together in anger he would fight it, and he does not value such an omen.
640.nuance: The verse is the king's refusal to be warned, and his own claim that the sages' word counts for little; the epic does not endorse it.

claims.claim: a brave king need not heed a petty word of omen

641.reading: The narrator says that the king, who saw no fault in any good man's deed, told fit counsellors to speak and let it be understood.
641.nuance: He calls counsel only after saying in 634 to 640 that he would fight regardless, so the order may be formal; the last two lines are read in this way.
641.event: The king orders his counsellors to speak and give their counsel.

642.reading: When the king of the garland and discus had said this, his learned counsellors, skilled in the work of the books, spoke to him with their own plans and gave him understanding.
642.nuance: The phrase for the counsellors' learning is hard to read, and the content of the advice is left to the following verses.
642.event: The counsellors answer the king with their own advice.

links.note: Kural 389 says the world rests under the umbrella of a king who can bear words bitter to the ear; verse 620 names a king by the opposite temper, striking in anger and unable to bear a word against him.
links.teaches: The couplet's virtue is given its negative portrait in a ruler whose pride goes with his intolerance.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure by which this temper counts as a failing, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a figure who embodies the opposite, which the verse supplies.

links.note: Kural 617 says the goddess of misfortune lives in sloth and the lotus goddess in the labour of the unslothful; in verse 621 the goddess of fortune takes offence and looks for another place, because the king has not come to her.
links.teaches: In the Kural fortune leaves a man for sloth; here she leaves a king for his pleasure, so the fault is attention given elsewhere.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying what kind of man keeps fortune, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of fortune as a slighted lover, which the verse gives.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 140 says the five senses come under one's control of themselves once one has met the Lord; verse 624 says a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer.
links.teaches: The epic gives self-conquest as a ruler's own work with a public reward; the Saiva stanza makes it follow from meeting the Lord.

gains.a: The verse lacks any account of how self-conquest comes about, since it names only its fruit.
gains.b: The stanza lacks a worldly payoff for the mastery it describes, which the verse gives in an unconquerable realm.

links.note: Kural 385 names a king as one able to create, gather, guard and apportion wealth; verse 626 gives the same four acts and says it is the learned man who becomes the protector of others.
links.teaches: The couplet's four tasks are tied to learning, so the verse makes the king's wealth-work depend on what he has studied.

gains.a: The verse lacks a compact statement that these four acts define rule, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the condition that only the learned can do it, which the verse adds.

links.note: Kural 431 says the wealth of those without arrogance, anger and smallness has a dignified quality; verse 627 makes arrogance a frost that destroys the lotus of wealth.
links.teaches: The couplet says what spoils the dignity of wealth; the verse shows how, with arrogance falling on wealth like frost on a lotus.

gains.a: The verse lacks the positive side, that wealth without arrogance keeps its dignity, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks an image of the ruin pride causes, which the verse supplies.

links.note: In 627 the astrologer warns that pride falls like frost on the lotus of wealth; in 634 the king, smiling, boasts that his shoulders have beaten the Vidyadhara kings and so he need fear no foe.
links.teaches: The warning is answered by the very boast it described, so the king's reply is what the astrologer's image forecasts.

links.note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants at the head of armies fall and change when their deeds turn against them; verse 635 has a king boasting that mere men cannot shake him.
links.teaches: A king's claim of strength is read as the very certainty that, in the Naladiyar, precedes the fall of such rulers.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard that sets his boast against what happens to powerful kings, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a living king speaking the boast it warns against, which the verse supplies.

links.note: In 402 the lord says that because of a girl he will take the life and the discus of Ashvagriva; in 638 the king names that very discus as the power by which he could cut down the shoulders of the gods.
links.teaches: The weapon the king trusts is the thing the earlier verse says will be taken from him with his life.

links.note: Verse 409 says the sign about the garlanded one means that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; verse 639 has the king ask whether the book of omens may be a deceit.
links.teaches: The king treats as doubtful the omen-book that the other court has already taken as certain, which is the difference between the two courts' fates.

links.note: Verse 402 says the lord will take the discus and life of Ashvagriva because of a girl; verse 632 has the astrologer call the youngest Podanam prince a foe of old.
links.teaches: The same prince is named as the threat from the rival's court that the earlier verse named as the taker of his life.

links.note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the king's eyes and he should take counsel; verse 641 has the king, who has already said he will fight regardless, tell his ministers to counsel.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule is shown with its limit, as counsel asked after the king has made up his mind.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying why counsellors matter, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where counsel is asked only to confirm the king's mind, which the verse shows.

source_issues: Verse 620 lines 2 and 3 (தேறின் யாரையும் தேறும்): the sense of the king's overconfidence is a best reading.
Verse 625: the phrases கோசிறண்டத்தன் and மாசிறண்டத்தன் are doubled and clipped; the sense is uncertain.
Verses 631 to 640: the verses do not name their speakers; the astrologer is taken as the speaker of 623 to 632 and the king of 634 to 640, from the story and the closing verbs.
Verse 639: the person addressed is not clear.
Verse 633 lines 1 to 2 and verse 642 lines 2 to 3 are corrupt or badly divided in the text.
